Fund cost records: reinvested distributions and return of capital can change the sale gain

Follow an invented non-registered mutual-fund ledger from opening purchase through reinvestment, cash return of capital and sale, keeping units, cost base and market value separate.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Follow one invented Canadian mutual-fund unit ledger in a non-registered account

Interactive planning lab

Adjusted cost base before selling all units$10,300
Units sold, including fractional reinvested units525
Capital gain or loss before any inclusion-rate calculation$1,230

One invented non-registered Canadian mutual-fund holding, one opening purchase, a fully reinvested taxable distribution, a later cash return of capital and one sale of every unit. The taxable distribution input is its actual cash-equivalent amount, not a dividend gross-up or income-tax amount. The post-distribution reinvestment NAV equals the entered opening purchase NAV by explicit assumption; the pre-distribution NAV is higher by distribution per original unit. Fractional units are allowed. Cash return of capital is retained outside and reduces NAV and ACB without changing units. Input limits keep NAV and ACB positive, so zero-basis and excess-return-of-capital rules are excluded. Selling expense reduces sale proceeds and is not deducted from ACB again. No taxes, inclusion rate, loss offsets, withholding, foreign currency, registered account, other identical holdings, additional trades or deemed dispositions are calculated. Intermediate book-cost and NAV stages are assumed, not observed fund performance. Calculations keep full precision until display.

On this page

  1. Keep the unit count, market value and cost base in separate records
  2. Add the actual amount reinvested and the units it purchases
  3. Record a later cash return of capital without buying more units
  4. Subtract adjusted cost and selling expenses once
  5. Do not confuse sale gain with all cash and value received
  6. Use complete transaction records before turning the illustration into a filing number

The central idea

Original cash invested is not always the current adjusted cost base. Reinvestment can add cost and units, while return of capital can reduce cost without changing the unit count.

01

Keep the unit count, market value and cost base in separate records

A fund statement can show the current value of an investment without explaining every adjustment needed for its cost record. The amount first paid, the units now owned and the adjusted cost base can change in different ways after distributions and later transactions.

Adjusted cost base, or ACB, is a cost measure used in calculating a capital gain or loss. It is not a continuously updated market valuation. A rise or fall in the quoted unit price does not by itself update that cost record.

The CRA’s mutual-fund guidance explains reinvested distributions, returns of capital and average cost for identical fund units. This article uses those mechanics in an independent non-registered illustration with one holding, rather than recreating an issuer’s transaction history or completing a tax return.

02

Add the actual amount reinvested and the units it purchases

The example buys 500 units at CAD 20 each, for an opening cost of CAD 10,000. It later receives a taxable distribution with an actual cash-equivalent amount of CAD 500, all of which is reinvested at a post-distribution NAV of CAD 20.

Reinvestment buys twenty-five additional units, taking the total to 525. Total cost increases by the amount used to acquire those units: CAD 10,000 + CAD 500 = CAD 10,500. The average cost remains CAD 20 per unit at this particular stage.

The illustration assumes a pre-distribution NAV of CAD 21 for the original 500 units. Paying CAD 1 per original unit transfers CAD 500 out of that value; immediate reinvestment at CAD 20 purchases the additional units. It does not create CAD 500 of value on top of a fund already worth CAD 10,500.

CRA also explains that reinvesting a distribution does not remove the applicable income-reporting requirement. The input is the actual amount reinvested, not a dividend gross-up, tax bill or assumed after-tax amount. Any tax funding would need its own cash ledger.

03

Record a later cash return of capital without buying more units

The next event is a CAD 200 return of capital paid in cash and retained outside the fund. It does not purchase additional units, so the holder still owns 525. It reduces total ACB from CAD 10,500 to CAD 10,300.

Average cost becomes approximately CAD 19.619048 per unit. The hypothetical market NAV also falls by CAD 200 divided by 525 units when that cash is transferred out. The grouped bars show book cost and NAV separately, even though they happen to coincide again after this event under the chosen assumptions.

That equality is not a general rule. An actual fund can have market gains or losses unrelated to its holder’s cost record. Likewise, a falling NAV alone cannot establish whether a payment is return of capital. Use the reported classification and relevant records rather than guessing the character from the price chart.

The controls keep total ACB positive. Cases where adjustments reach or pass zero require additional rules and are outside this example. The displayed per-unit values are rounded; calculations retain full precision rather than rebuilding the total cost from a rounded per-unit label.

04

Subtract adjusted cost and selling expenses once

The final sale redeems all 525 units at CAD 22, producing gross proceeds of CAD 11,550. A separately entered CAD 20 selling expense leaves net proceeds of CAD 11,530.

The capital gain before any inclusion-rate calculation is CAD 11,550 − CAD 20 − CAD 10,300 = CAD 1,230. The selling expense is subtracted once from proceeds. It is not also deducted from ACB as another adjustment.

Using only the original CAD 10,000 purchase cost would produce a CAD 1,530 gain on the same net proceeds. That shortcut overstates the result by CAD 300, which equals the net cost-base increase from CAD 500 reinvested less CAD 200 returned.

The signed comparison shows both calculations and their difference. Depending on the entered adjustments, ignoring later cost changes can either overstate or understate a gain. A negative calculated sale result is simply a loss amount here; the tool does not determine whether or how it can be used for tax purposes.

05

Do not confuse sale gain with all cash and value received

The retained CAD 200 return of capital is outside the fund before the final sale. Adding it to CAD 11,530 of net sale proceeds gives CAD 11,730 of remaining resources before any tax, compared with CAD 10,000 originally supplied.

That CAD 1,730 resource increase is different from the CAD 1,230 sale gain because the illustration also included the earlier CAD 500 distribution. The distribution and later sale gain are different events. Their tax treatment is not calculated by adding the two as though every income category had the same rules.

The return of capital itself is not new investment profit added on top of all other returns. It transferred value into outside cash and reduced the cost base. Counting it again as extra profit while ignoring that adjustment would disconnect the cash and cost records.

The matrix varies sale NAV and the cash return-of-capital amount. Each cell is a separate complete ledger, with the same opening purchase, reinvested distribution and selling expense. It is not a prediction of prices or a sequence of additional payments.

06

Use complete transaction records before turning the illustration into a filing number

The calculation assumes no other identical holdings, purchases, partial sales, transfers, foreign-currency amounts or adjustments. Real records can be more involved. The CRA guidance discusses average cost for identical units in the same fund class or series, rather than treating every purchase as an isolated lot selected after the fact.

Reconcile the relevant transaction history, distribution records and cost-base adjustments. A quoted market value, the first bank transfer or one sale slip may not supply every amount needed. Confirm the applicable scope of identical holdings when records span more than one account.

This article stops at the gain or loss before any inclusion-rate calculation. It supplies no personal tax rate, allowable-loss assessment, refund or after-tax spending amount. Its purpose is to make the cost record inspectable before those separate tax and planning questions are answered.
